nameStory: The 'thimbleweed' name comes from the plant's distinctive fuzzy, rounded seed head that looks just like an old-fashioned sewing thimble! After the white flowers fade away, this charming little 'thimble' sits atop the stem, packed with woolly seeds ready to catch the wind. It's also called 'tall' thimbleweed because it can reach nearly three feet high, towering over its shorter thimbleweed cousins.
description: Tall thimbleweed is a sturdy wildflower that stands 1-3 feet tall in New England's woodlands and clearings. It produces simple white flowers in late spring and early summer, but its real claim to fame is the fuzzy, thimble-shaped seed head that follows. The leaves are deeply divided and arranged in a distinctive whorl (circle) around the middle of the stem, giving the plant an orderly, geometric appearance. This tough native perennial can handle both drought and cold, making it a reliable woodland resident.

idTips.label: Fruit/Seeds
idTips.description: The gray-white, thimble-shaped seed head is unmistakable - about the size of your thumb tip and covered in dense, woolly fuzz that feels soft to the touch. Seeds blow away like tiny parachutes when ripe.

idTips.label: Leaves
idTips.description: Three deeply cut leaves arranged in a perfect whorl (circle) halfway up the stem, like nature's chandelier. Each leaf feels slightly rough and has jagged, finger-like divisions.

idTips.label: Flowers
idTips.description: Simple white or greenish-white flowers with 5 petal-like sepals, blooming May through July. No true petals - what looks like petals are actually sepals that feel papery thin.

idTips.label: Growth Habit
idTips.description: Stands upright and unbranched, typically 1-3 feet tall with a single stem. Often grows in small colonies connected by underground roots.

idTips.label: Stem
idTips.description: Smooth, green stem that feels firm and slightly ridged when you run your finger along it. No branches - just one straight shot up to the flower.

habitat: Look for tall thimbleweed in dry, open woodlands, woodland edges, and clearings throughout New England. It thrives in well-drained, slightly acidic soils and can handle both partial shade and sunny spots. You'll often find it growing alongside other woodland wildflowers in oak-hickory forests or in areas where the forest canopy has been opened by natural disturbance.

seasonality.spring: New growth emerges in late spring with the characteristic whorl of leaves appearing first, followed by flower buds in May.
seasonality.summer: White flowers bloom from May through July, gradually giving way to the developing green seed heads that will become the fuzzy 'thimbles.'
seasonality.fall: The distinctive gray-white, woolly seed heads are at their most prominent and begin releasing their wind-dispersed seeds.
seasonality.winter: Dead stems may persist with dried seed heads still attached, though most seeds have blown away by late winter.

funFact: Despite being called a 'tumbleweed' by some, tall thimbleweed doesn't actually tumble like a classic tumbleweed - instead, its individual seeds act like tiny paratroopers, each equipped with its own fluffy parachute to drift away on the breeze!
confusionNotes: The white flowers might remind you of wood anemone, but tall thimbleweed's whorl of three deeply cut leaves halfway up the stem is a dead giveaway - wood anemone has different leaf arrangements and grows much shorter.
contextualKnowledge: Don't let the 'tumbleweed' nickname fool you - this is a well-behaved New England native, not the invasive rolling tumbleweed of western movies. Several different plants share the 'thimbleweed' name, so the distinctive leaf whorl and height help distinguish this particular species.
compareHints: Tall thimbleweed stands out from its relatives by its height and that distinctive whorl of three deeply cut leaves halfway up the stem. Cutleaf anemone is much shorter and has different leaf arrangements, while cylindrical thimbleweed has a more elongated, cylinder-shaped seed head rather than the rounded thimble shape. The whorled leaves are really your best field mark for identifying this particular species.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Unlike its New England relatives tall thimbleweed and cylindrical thimbleweed, cutleaf anemone has much more finely divided, lacy leaves rather than broader, coarsely toothed ones.
Cylindrical thimbleweed differs from its relative tall thimbleweed by its distinctly elongated, narrow seed head versus the latter's more rounded, globe-shaped one.
